Concentration name: Global Africa and the Diaspora, Gender, Sexuality and Women's Studies, Urban Studies, Law and Society
description: The Africana Studies major is an interdisciplinary major in the humanities and social sciences that is designed to provide students with an understanding of the history, culture, and social realities of people of African descent. Majors in Africana Studies are expected to develop a sophisticated understanding of the theoretical and methodological issues that inform the field. They are also expected to demonstrate a solid familiarity with the key historical moments, intellectual movements, and social struggles that have shaped the discipline. The Africana Studies major requires a minimum of 14 course units. We encourage students to double-major, as Africana Studies provides a unique perspective to students who major in other disciplines, from English to Economics, and from Psychology to Biology.

The major in ancient history is an interdisciplinary major, sponsored by the Departments of Classical Studies and History. All majors are assigned an advisor from one of the two departments and should consult with their advisor on a regular basis. The major is an appropriate background for many fields and professions, including law and medicine, and for graduate work in history, classics, archaeology, and other related disciplines. There are two concentrations, one in Greek and Roman history, the other in Near Eastern history.

Concentration name: Archaeology Concentration, Biological Anthropology Concentration, Cultural and Linguistic Anthropology Concentration, Medical Anthropology and Global Health Concentration
description: The Anthropology major introduces students to the comparative study of human diversity and the critical analysis of the concept of "culture." The discipline is conventionally divided into four sub-fields: cultural anthropology, linguistic anthropology, biological anthropology, and archaeology. At Penn, we offer courses in all four sub-fields as well as in medical anthropology. Students may choose to concentrate in any one of the following four areas: Archaeology, Biological Anthropology, Cultural and Linguistic Anthropology, or Medical Anthropology and Global Health.

The undergraduate major in architecture is a liberal arts degree in the College of Arts and Sciences. The major gives students a deep and broad understanding of architecture as a cultural practice. Students learn about architecture’s history, theories and technologies in the context of global cultures. They also become proficient in the skills needed to represent architectural ideas, including drawing, modeling, and digital software. With its strong and diverse curriculum, the major prepares students for graduate studies in architecture and its allied disciplines of landscape architecture, urban planning and historic preservation. It also provides a strong foundation for students who want to pursue careers in a wide range of fields from law and business to engineering, public policy and the visual arts.

Biochemistry is the study of the chemistry of life. It provides the foundation for the revolutionary developments in biotechnology and genetic engineering that are having a major impact in areas ranging from medicine to forensics to bioremediation. Biochemistry majors study the major classes of biological molecules: proteins, nucleic acids, lipids and carbohydrates. They learn the chemical principles that underlie the function of these molecules in the processes that sustain life. All biochemistry majors do a two-semester research project with a faculty preceptor. The major is appropriate for students interested in careers in the biological and chemical sciences as well as in the health professions. There is a BS and a BA version of the major. The BA degree is designed for students who want a somewhat less intensive science program than the BS biochemistry major, perhaps because they want to combine it with a second major or because they want more elective time for other courses, perhaps in the arts and humanities. The BA degree can also serve as preparation for careers in industry or public service.

The Bachelor of Arts (BA) with a major in Biology is intended for students who are interested in biology but do not plan to attend graduate school in the life sciences or a health professions school. Students in the College of Arts and Sciences may complete a major in Biology for the BA degree. The requirements are distinct from those for the Bachelor of Arts degree with a major in Biology that may be completed by students in the College of Liberal and Professional Studies. Requirements for the major are listed below. In addition, students must complete the General Requirement of the College of Arts and Sciences.

Biophysics is an interdisciplinary field that applies the theories and methods of physics, chemistry, and mathematics to understand how biological systems work. Its scope is vast, covering all scales of biological organization, from the single molecule to the cell, from the organism to the ecosystem. Biophysics has grown very rapidly in recent years, leading to new opportunities for careers at the cutting edge of science. Undergraduates who major in biophysics at Penn can participate fully in this excitement through research. They will acquire a solid foundation in the physical and life sciences that will prepare them for a variety of careers in scientific research, medicine, and the biotechnology industry. The Biophysics Major is appropriate for students who are planning graduate study in biophysics or a related area, such as molecular biology or neuroscience, or the professional schools of medicine, dentistry, or law.

The Department of Chemistry offers several majors to accommodate student interests. The Bachelor of Arts (BA) major is less intensive than the Bachelor of Science (BS) majors and is designed for those students who desire a strong background in chemistry but who do not intend to pursue graduate school in chemistry. The BA in chemistry is also an excellent option for those who have a double major. In addition to chemistry majors, we also offer submatriculation programs for master’s degrees in chemistry and in education, as well as a minor in chemistry.

The undergraduate program in Cinema and Media Studies provides students with a comprehensive understanding of the history, theory, and aesthetics of moving images. Students learn to analyze film, television, and new media in a variety of contexts, considering their formal properties as well as their relationship to culture, society, and technology. The major emphasizes critical thinking, close analysis, and strong writing skills. Courses cover a wide range of topics, including silent cinema, Hollywood genres, international film movements, documentary, animation, television studies, and digital media. Students have the opportunity to explore filmmaking through production courses and to gain practical experience through internships. The program prepares students for careers in the film and media industries, as well as for graduate study in related fields.

Concentration name: Classical Languages and Literature, Classical Civilization, Ancient History, Mediterranean Archaeology
description: The Classical Studies major offers a multi-disciplinary approach to the study of the ancient Greek and Roman worlds, allowing students to explore the interconnected cultures of the ancient Mediterranean. Students in the Classical Studies major can take courses in the art, archaeology, history, literature, and philosophy of the ancient Greek and Roman worlds, and can also study the ancient Greek and Latin languages. Because of the multi-disciplinary nature of the major, students who major in Classical Studies will learn how to synthesize a wide variety of evidence (textual, material, visual, etc.) and thus prepare themselves for a wide range of future careers.

Concentration name: Language; Mind, Brain and Behavior; Cognitive Neuroscience; Computation and Cognition; Psychology: Mind, Brain and Behavior; Language and the Mind
description: Cognitive Science is the study of the mind and its processes. It is an interdisciplinary field, combining results and insights from psychology, computer science, linguistics, philosophy, and neuroscience. Work in cognitive science has had a major impact on our understanding of language, perception, action, memory, reasoning, decision making, emotion, and consciousness; it has also led to the design of intelligent systems that can perform complex tasks that formerly required human intelligence.

Concentration name: Communication and Public Service (ComPS), Communication, Culture, and Media, Political Communication, Data and Network Science, Critical Journalism
description: The undergraduate program in Communication is rooted in the liberal arts tradition, providing a broad understanding of the role of communication in society, and a critical framework for analyzing communication institutions, processes, and effects. The curriculum is designed to help students think systematically about communication and to express those thoughts clearly. Courses in the major examine communication from a variety of theoretical and methodological perspectives. They offer students the knowledge and analytical skills to understand and evaluate communication theories and research. Communication majors have the option of selecting a concentration within the major.

The major in Comparative Literature allows students to bring together their passion for the literatures and cultures of different parts of the world. As a discipline, Comparative Literature is founded on the belief that literary texts can only be fully understood in a comparative framework. This means that at Penn, students not only take courses in a variety of literary traditions, they also learn how to think comparatively about what they read. The major has two main components: coursework in Comparative Literature and coursework in two foreign literature departments. In their Comparative Literature courses, students learn how to analyze and compare texts from a variety of theoretical, historical, and generic perspectives. In their foreign literature courses, students develop the in-depth knowledge of individual literary traditions and languages that all true comparative work requires. The flexibility of the major allows students to shape their own program of study in consultation with the undergraduate chair.

The Criminology major is an interdisciplinary program that focuses on the problem of crime and the criminal justice system. The curriculum draws on a wide variety of disciplines, including Criminology, Sociology, History, Law, and Political Science. The major is designed for students interested in studying the causes and consequences of crime, the structure and function of the criminal justice system, and the social, cultural, and political contexts of law and justice. The major provides a strong foundation for students interested in careers in law, criminal justice, public policy, and social service, as well as for graduate study in Criminology, Sociology, or Law.

Concentration name: Art, Technology, and the Future; City and Social Change; Communication, Information, and Media; Mind and Materiality
description: The undergraduate major in Design leads to a BA degree in the College of Arts and Sciences. The major combines hands-on-making with a critical and historical framing of design. The major emphasizes critical thinking and creative production and offers a curriculum that is both broad and deep, allowing students flexibility to follow their own interests and develop a unique course of study. The major requires 13 courses: five core courses in design and four courses in a specific concentration that builds on the foundations of the core. Two studio courses and two seminar/lecture courses in a concentration provide students with depth and a critical framework for understanding their work. Two additional electives, from any concentration, and two major-related courses, complete the major. Students take a final thesis course in the fall of their senior year. This course prepares them for a capstone project that is presented to the public in a final exhibition at the end of the spring semester.

The major in Earth Science focuses on the Earth as a complex system, and includes a solid foundation in the core disciplines of geology, biology,chemistry, and physics. The Bachelor of Arts (BA) in Earth and Environmental Science is intended for students who wish to pursue a career or graduate work in environmental policy, environmental law, management, journalism, or education. It provides a broad background in Earth and Environmental Science, and some flexibility in the selection of upper-level courses.

The major in East Asian Languages and Civilizations (EALC) provides students with a broad and deep understanding of the cultures of East Asia (China, Japan, and Korea). The curriculum is designed to provide students with the linguistic competency, disciplinary methodology, and factual knowledge to pursue a professional career or graduate studies in a field related to East Asia. The program has three key components: language training, broad foundational coursework in the humanities and social sciences, and a specialization in one area of East Asian studies. In consultation with the undergraduate chair, students build a program of study that is at once comprehensive and tailored to their own intellectual interests. The language component requires four years of Chinese, Japanese, or Korean. The foundational coursework gives students a broad overview of the history, literature, and cultures of East Asia. The specialization gives students the opportunity to bring their linguistic and disciplinary training to bear on one particular area of interest. In order to achieve the goals of the major, students are required to take a minimum of sixteen courses: eight in language and eight in non-language content courses. These requirements are described in more detail below. Students are encouraged to take advantage of Penn’s many study abroad programs, as well as the full range of courses in EALC and related departments and programs.
Program name: East Asian Languages and Civilizations, BA

Concentration name: Advanced Theory Concentration, Data Analytics Concentration, Finance Concentration, International Economics Concentration, Public Policy Concentration, Behavioral Economics Concentration, Strategic Management Concentration, Individualized Concentration
description: The undergraduate economics major is designed to provide students with a firm grounding in modern economic theory, statistical and econometric methods, and their applications. It is designed to be flexible, allowing students to construct a program of study that suits their interests and goals. Students in the major may go on to graduate school in economics, law, medicine, or business; others take jobs in government, private firms, or the non-profit sector. An important part of the economics major is the senior research requirement, in which students have an opportunity to engage in economic research under the supervision of a faculty member.

Concentration name: American Literature and Culture, British and Other Anglophone Literature, Cinema and Media Studies, Creative Writing, Generalist, Genre and Poetics, Global and Transnational English, Literature and Culture before the 17th Century, Literature and Culture from the 17th Century to the Present, Theoretical and Cross-Cultural Studies
description: The English major at Penn offers an opportunity to study a rich variety of literary, cultural, and historical documents, from ancient epics to contemporary films. Our department includes many distinguished scholars who are also dedicated teachers. Our courses are typically small and stress active student participation. Students are encouraged to develop their own interests and to work closely with faculty members in directed readings and honors projects. The major itself combines a focus on traditional historical fields with a wide range of theoretical and interdisciplinary pursuits. It has long enjoyed an international reputation in areas such as Renaissance literature, American literature, modernism, and contemporary poetry. It has also emerged as a vital center for the study of ethnic literature, gender and sexuality studies, cultural studies, and critical theory. The English major helps students to become perceptive readers, critical thinkers, and strong writers—skills that provide a foundation for careers in a wide range of professions, including law, business, publishing, journalism, education, and the arts.

The Environmental Studies major provides students with the intellectual and practical tools to understand and address pressing environmental challenges. The major attracts a diverse group of students who are curious about the many intersections between human societies and the biophysical environment, and prepares them to pursue careers in a wide array of fields. The interdisciplinary nature of the major enables students to integrate knowledge from across the humanities, social sciences, and natural sciences, and our emphasis on experiential learning—including field courses, undergraduate research, study abroad, internships, and civic engagement—gives students hands-on opportunities to apply their knowledge. Students in the major select one of seven concentrations, each of which has a distinct curriculum and area of focus. We also offer a General major option for students with an interest in Environmental Studies but whose academic interests do not fit well with any of the defined concentrations. All Environmental Studies majors take an introductory course (ENVS 1000), a statistics course, and a senior seminar in which they complete an independent research project that integrates their coursework with their concentration. For College students, the Environmental Studies major fulfills the Natural Science & Math requirement of the Sector Requirement.

The undergraduate major in Fine Arts is intended for students who wish to pursue a rigorous liberal arts education and a studio-based visual arts curriculum. Students may work in a variety of disciplines, including animation and 3D modeling, drawing, painting, photography, printmaking, sculpture, and video. Through a combination of core studios, art history courses, and a wide array of studio electives, the curriculum provides an open intellectual framework that allows for a deep and broad-based investigation into the practice of making art today.

The major in Francophone, Italian and Germanic Studies (FIGS) allows students to study the cultures of the French-, Italian- and German-speaking worlds from a comparative and interdisciplinary perspective. This major is ideal for students with an interest in two of these three areas. A major that combines two of the three subjects allows students to develop an intercultural perspective that enhances their understanding of both fields. The FIGS major consists of twelve courses, six in a primary language and culture and four in a secondary language and culture, plus two additional electives that can come from either area. In consultation with the FIGS advisor, each student will design a course of study that reflects their interests in the language, literature, history and culture of the Francophone, Italian and German-speaking worlds. Courses are taught in English and in the target languages. FIGS majors who wish to study abroad are encouraged to do so and can count courses taken abroad toward their major requirements.
Program name: Francophone, Italian and Germanic Studies, BA

Concentration name: Feminist Studies, Global Gender and Sexuality Studies, Health and Disability, Individualized Concentration
description: The undergraduate program in Gender, Sexuality, and Women’s Studies (GSWS) offers students the opportunity to pursue interdisciplinary study in a variety of fields concerned with gender, sexuality, and women. Students learn to think critically about the social construction of gender and the ways in which gender and sexuality have been defined and have operated in various historical and cultural contexts. The major is broadly interdisciplinary and requires students to take courses in the humanities, social sciences, and policy-oriented fields. The GSWS major is flexible, with a required core of introductory, theory, and research courses and many options for electives in several areas of concentration.

Concentration name: Bioethics and Society, Disease and Society, Gender, Sexuality and Health, Global Health, Health Care Markets and Finance, Health Policy and Law, Race, Ethnicity and Health
description: The Health and Societies (HSOC) major provides students with a multi-disciplinary framework for understanding the social, cultural, political, economic, and ethical dimensions of health, illness, and medical care in human societies, past and present. The curriculum is designed to help students think critically about the complex relationships that link health to social and cultural contexts. All students majoring in Health & Societies choose a concentration within the major. Concentrations enable students to acquire a deeper understanding of a specific facet of the major and to hone their analytical skills by working closely with a faculty member in their area of interest. Concentrations consist of four courses. Students also complete a capstone course in their senior year.

The major in Hispanic Studies offers a broad and comprehensive curriculum in the literatures and cultures of the Spanish-speaking world: Spain, Latin America and the U.S. Courses are taught in Spanish. The curriculum combines broad survey courses with more specialized courses on specific topics, periods, authors and genres. Students are required to develop a comprehensive knowledge of Hispanic literatures and cultures from the Middle Ages to the present, as well as the analytical skills to engage critically with primary and secondary texts. Students majoring in Hispanic Studies also have the option of declaring a concentration in Portuguese and Brazilian Studies, which provides a more specialized curricular path including two required courses and several electives.

Concentration name: Architecture Concentration, General History of Art Concentration, Museums, Markets and Collecting Concentration, History of Art Honors Program with Thesis
description: The History of Art major is intended to provide students with a broad and deep understanding of the history of art and architecture of a variety of periods and geographical areas, and to equip them with the tools of visual and historical analysis necessary to make a contribution to the field. Majors are encouraged to pursue an interdisciplinary and global course of study and to take advantage of the rich offerings across the university as they craft a personalized program of courses that will culminate in a capstone seminar. The capstone seminar is an intensive research and writing course designed to familiarize students with the most advanced methods in the discipline and to produce a substantial research paper. For students considering graduate work in the field, for those interested in museum or gallery work, and for those who simply wish to explore a particular area of art history in depth, the department offers a variety of specialized concentrations, as well as an honors program that provides an in-depth and challenging course of study.

The History Major is designed to stimulate and gratify students' curiosity about the past, to sharpen their critical and analytical skills, and to provide them with intellectual perspectives that will be of great value whatever their future pursuits. Students have maximum freedom in the choice of their courses, but the Major's requirements are meant to ensure that their choices are both coherent and broad. We especially want our students to think about the nature of history itself. The Proseminar, the Research Seminar and the optional Honors Thesis all emphasize historiographical issues as well as research methods.

The Individualized Major allows students to combine courses from several departments and programs into a coherent field of study not represented in any of the College’s established majors. The major is interdepartmental and interdisciplinary in nature. A student must have a cumulative GPA of 3.0 or above to apply for an Individualized Major. Students interested in this major should meet with a College advisor to discuss their ideas and to begin to search for a faculty advisor. The application to the major should be submitted by the end of sophomore year.

Concentration name: Commercial & Legal Institutions of the World Economy Track, Conflict & Security Track, Foreign Policy & Diplomacy Track, Global Governance & International Organizations Track, Global Health & Environment Track, International Political Economy & Development Track, Latin American & Caribbean Studies Track, Middle Eastern & North African Studies Track, Russian & East European Studies Track, South Asian Studies Track, Sub-Saharan African Studies Track, United States in the World Track, Western European Studies Track
description: The International Relations (IR) Program at Penn is an interdisciplinary major in the College of Arts and Sciences that is jointly administered by the Political Science Department and the Lauder Institute. We offer an undergraduate education in world politics that is balanced, comprehensive, and rigorous. Students investigate the political, economic, and cultural interactions of a wide range of state and non-state actors at the local, national, and international levels. Students become familiar with the historical evolution of the international system and its current-day workings while engaging questions of ethics, justice, and the distribution of power. The IR major requires that students demonstrate a proficiency in a foreign language and complete a study abroad experience. In addition, we encourage our students to seek out internships that will help them gain first-hand experience in a variety of international fields and professions.

The International Studies Major (ISMA) is a joint major with the Wharton School that provides students with the opportunity to combine a business education with a liberal arts focus on international studies. Students complete the full Wharton curriculum as well as 14-course units in the College of Arts & Sciences. These courses include language proficiency as well as area studies and international relations coursework. The major allows students to choose a concentration in a particular geographic region of the world: Africa, Asia, Europe, or Latin America. This joint major is only open to students admitted to the Huntsman Program.

The Jewish Studies Program at the University of Pennsylvania provides a comprehensive, multi-disciplinary approach to Jewish civilization from antiquity to the present. As an academic field, Jewish studies is anchored in the traditional humanities—in the mastery of languages and the close reading of texts from a wide variety of genres—but it has also come to embrace the full gamut of approaches of the social sciences. The Jewish studies major will provide the basic tools for all students to pursue this inter-disciplinary field while encouraging each to develop his or her specific interests. This major can be an excellent preparation for careers in Jewish education, the rabbinate, Jewish communal service, and graduate work in Jewish studies. For students whose main interests lie elsewhere, a major in Jewish Studies will also constitute a superb liberal arts education and an unusually rich opportunity to explore questions of history, literature, religion, and culture that have broad applicability to other fields.

The Latin American and Latinx Studies (LALS) Program offers an interdisciplinary major and minor to students in the College of Arts and Sciences. LALS offers students the opportunity to learn about the diverse histories, politics, economies, and cultures of the region as well as those of its peoples in the U.S. By combining courses offered in several departments, LALS introduces students to the study of Latin America and the Caribbean, while also providing them with the opportunity to specialize in one or two disciplines and/or one or two areas of the region. A certificate in LALS is available for Wharton undergraduates, and a minor for undergraduates in the Schools of Engineering and Applied Science and Nursing. Penn undergraduates in all four schools can get a language certificate in Portuguese, Quechua or Spanish.

Concentration name: Law and Social Structure, Law and Social Change, Global and Comparative Law
description: The Law and Society major provides an interdisciplinary and multidisciplinary liberal arts approach to the study of law and legal institutions, and their impact on society. In this major, law is studied as a social institution, in the context of both the humanities and the social sciences. Students are encouraged to develop a critical understanding of legal institutions, and of law in its social, cultural, and historical contexts. Law and Society majors take a core set of courses offered by the Sociology Department, and then select courses from Sociology and from several other departments in the College of Arts and Sciences, and from the Wharton School. Students are introduced to the various modes of inquiry used in legal studies, including historical, philosophical, and social science approaches.

Concentration name: Concentration in American Sign Language and Deaf Studies (ASLD)
Concentration in Language and Social Structure
Concentration in Language and the Brain
description: Linguistics is the scientific study of human language. It is a multifaceted discipline that addresses the structure of language (phonetics, phonology, morphology, syntax, and semantics) as well as the social and cultural aspects of language (sociolinguistics, historical linguistics), how language is acquired (language acquisition), and how it is represented in the mind (psycholinguistics, neurolinguistics). A major in linguistics offers an excellent basis for a variety of careers in fields such as education, computer science, psychology, law, and many other fields.

The Logic, Information, and Computation (LGIC) major, administered by the Department of Mathematics, is an interdisciplinary major that provides students with a strong foundation in the core principles of logic, computation, and information, especially as they are applied in mathematics, computer science, linguistics, and philosophy. The LGIC major is designed to appeal to students with a variety of interests, since the major allows students to choose one of four concentrations: Cognitive Science (LGIC-COGS), Computation and Logic (LGIC-COMP), Logic and Language (LGIC-LANG), and Mathematical Logic (LGIC-MATH).

The Mathematical Economics major is an interdepartmental major between the Economics Department (in the School of Arts and Sciences) and the Statistics and Data Science Department (in the Wharton School). The major is very challenging and is suitable only for those students with a strong interest in and an aptitude for mathematics. The major seeks to endow the student with the basic tools of the professional economist. It provides an excellent background for graduate study in economics. Mathematical Economics is a major in the College of Arts and Sciences. It does not lead to a degree from the Wharton School.

Concentration name: Applied Mathematics and Computational Science Concentration
description: The major in Mathematics is intended for students who are interested in mathematics and its applications. It is also for those who plan to pursue graduate work in mathematics, or in such related fields as statistics, operations research, computer science, economics, finance, or business. For those interested primarily in applications or in the teaching of mathematics, it is possible to specialize in those areas. Flexibility is the keynote of the mathematics major. Please see the Mathematics Department website for more information.

The major in Middle Eastern Languages and Cultures is designed for students who seek a linguistically-grounded and interdisciplinary approach to the study of the Middle East. The major builds upon the language and culture foundation of the area of the student's primary language of study. Students will choose one of the five languages taught in the department as a focus language: Arabic, Hebrew, Hindi/Urdu, Persian, or Turkish. Students will take two advanced language courses beyond the language requirement, and a total of ten courses that count toward the major. Majors are required to take NELC 0100 Introduction to the Middle East, as well as a senior research seminar, NELC 3000, in which they will produce a capstone research paper. The remaining six courses will consist of departmentally-approved courses, three of which must be at the 2000-level or higher.

Concentration name: Anthropology and Sociology of the Middle East, History of the Middle East, Islamic Studies, Politics of the Middle East
description: The major in Modern Middle Eastern Studies (MMES) offers a course of study for students interested in the politics, history, religion, languages, and cultures of the region. This interdisciplinary major provides an opportunity for students to study the Middle East using the methodologies of various departments, including Anthropology, History, History of Art, Near Eastern Languages and Civilizations, Political Science, and Religious Studies. Majors receive thorough grounding in the history and politics of the modern Middle East, gain proficiency in a Middle Eastern language, and take a sequence of courses organized around one of four distinct concentrations: Anthropology and Sociology, History, Islamic Studies, and Politics. The major is designed to provide a sound liberal arts background for students interested in pursuing graduate studies or in careers in which a knowledge of the Middle East is essential, such as diplomacy, government, journalism, and business.

The Music major at Penn is designed to allow students to explore music from a variety of perspectives. The curriculum develops students' musicianship skills while offering a background in a variety of musical traditions and repertoires. Students majoring in music explore the cultural and historical contexts of music, as well as the theoretical and compositional techniques that underlie musical works. Music majors gain a strong background in music while also receiving a broad liberal arts education. This prepares them for graduate study in music, as well as for careers in many fields, including arts administration, business, education, law, medicine, music criticism and journalism, and performance, as well as other related areas.

Neuroscience is an interdisciplinary major that provides a strong background for students interested in the biological bases of thought and behavior. The curriculum is intended for students who wish to pursue graduate work in neuroscience, medicine, or related fields, and to provide the appropriate science background for other professions such as law, business, and education. Required courses are drawn from biology, chemistry, mathematics, physics, and psychology.

Nutrition science is the study of how food affects the body. It covers a wide range of topics, from the biochemical processes involved in metabolism to the social and behavioral factors that influence food choices. The Nutrition Science major at Penn is a basic science-based curriculum that prepares students for careers in medicine and other health professions, biomedical research, and public health. All students in the Nutrition Science major must complete the pre-med requirements. Our graduates are competitive candidates for medical, dental, and other health professional schools. Graduates of the program are also well prepared for graduate study leading to research, and for positions in industry, government, and other institutions that require a strong science background. All students in the Nutrition Science major take courses in chemistry, biology, physics, and math to establish a solid foundation in the basic sciences. Students in the major also take a sequence of three nutrition courses, including NUTR 1000 Nutrition and the Consumer, NUTR 2000 Nutrition and Metabolism, and NUTR 3300 Nutrition and the Life Cycle. Through these courses, students will gain an understanding of the functions of nutrients, the metabolic and physiologic consequences of nutrient deficiencies and excesses in human populations, and the role of nutrition in health and disease.

The major in philosophy is designed to acquaint students with the fundamentals of philosophical reasoning and to provide them with a sophisticated understanding of the major figures and periods in the history of philosophy, as well as the central problems and areas of the discipline in the present day. Through their coursework, students will develop and hone their abilities to think and write with clarity, rigor, and intellectual imagination. The Department encourages its majors to pursue a broad liberal arts education, and many of our students double-major in a variety of other fields. For those who choose to continue their philosophical studies in graduate school, we offer a rich and demanding curriculum; however, the philosophy major also provides an excellent preparation for many other professions, including law, medicine, business, and public service.

Concentration name: Choice, Behavior and Markets, Constitutionalism and Governance, Distributive Justice, Globalization, Public Policy and a Fourth Course
description: The Philosophy, Politics and Economics (PPE) major has a long and distinguished history. It was born at Oxford University in the 1920s out of the conviction that study of the great modern works of social, political, and economic thought would be a good preparation for students entering the civil service and public life. It has since become a highly successful and influential program of study around the world. The PPE major at Penn provides a multidisciplinary education to students who want to become leaders in public affairs and in the national and international business communities. The major rests on the view that an understanding of the contemporary world requires knowledge of the principles of economic and political science, informed by the rigor of philosophical thought.

The Physics B.A. is a more flexible program for students who may be interested in a career in medicine, law, business, education, or other fields. Although the B.A. degree may be sufficient to qualify students for some positions in industry or government, it is not usually considered adequate preparation for doctoral study in physics. It can, however, provide an excellent background for graduate work in other sciences.

The Undergraduate Program in Political Science is one of the largest undergraduate majors in the School of Arts and Sciences. It is also one of the most distinguished. Its faculty have international reputations, are leaders in their respective fields, and have been recognized both by the American Political Science Association and the University of Pennsylvania for their distinguished research and their teaching excellence. Our goal is to provide students with a deep and comprehensive understanding of politics. Politics is the process through which societies make collective decisions and determine how to distribute power and resources. The study of politics at Penn therefore encompasses a very broad range of topics, including: the meaning of democracy, the nature of personal liberty, the causes of war and peace, the sources of political and economic development, the challenges of environmental protection, the role of international organizations, the determinants of election outcomes, the nature of public opinion, and the meaning of justice and equality. To address these and other important questions, we offer an array of courses organized around four broad subfields of Political Science: American Politics, Comparative Politics, International Relations, and Political Theory.

Concentration name: Cognitive Neuroscience, Clinical & Positive Psychology, Social & Personality Psychology
description: Psychology is a science devoted to understanding human behavior, and the major at Penn is designed to give students an understanding of the important questions, methodologies, and findings in the major areas of this diverse field. Core course requirements ensure that students are exposed to the social, cognitive, developmental, and biological bases of behavior, and develop skills in the research methods and statistical techniques that are used to advance our understanding of these topics. Advanced coursework allows students to explore areas of personal interest in greater depth. Students are also encouraged to get involved in the research of the department by taking independent study courses with faculty members, or through paid research assistantships.

What is religion? How can we best study it? The major and minor in Religious Studies provide students with the opportunity to explore the variety of religious traditions, and to learn different methods and approaches to understanding them. The Religious Studies curriculum reflects a wide spectrum of historical and cultural traditions, ranging from the ancient Near East to modern America, from the Abrahamic faiths of Judaism, Christianity, and Islam to the religions of Asia and Africa. The curriculum also introduces majors and minors to a variety of theories and methods to study those religious traditions. In the major, each student works with a faculty advisor to develop a course of study that reflects the student's own particular interests, while also meeting the requirements of the major. The major thus offers a well-defined structure, but also considerable flexibility. As they take a range of courses in the department, students become acquainted with religious phenomena and learn about various scholarly approaches to the academic study of religion (e.g., historical, anthropological, sociological, philosophical, literary, etc.). Religious Studies majors and minors develop the ability to read analytically, think critically, and write cogently. They also gain the specific skills to apply these abilities to the cross-cultural study of religion in its historical context, as well as the contemporary role of religion in global affairs.

Concentration name: Russian Language, Literature, and Culture; Russian and East European Studies
description: The major in Russian and East European Studies offers a choice of two concentrations: Russian Language, Literature, and Culture; and Russian and East European Studies. The major in REES is designed to provide B.A. candidates with a broad, interdisciplinary background in the languages, literatures, cultures, and histories of Russia and Eastern Europe, and a more specific focus for those who intend to go on to an M.A. or Ph.D. program in these fields. Students who complete the major requirements will acquire significant reading and speaking ability in one or two of the region's languages; a sophisticated understanding of the historical, cultural, and social forces that have shaped Russia and Eastern Europe; and the research, analytical, and writing skills that are necessary for advanced work in the humanities and social sciences. Students are strongly encouraged to study abroad in Russia or Eastern Europe for at least one semester or a summer. The Russian and East European Studies Program is an undergraduate component of the Department of Russian and East European Studies. The department's program in Russian and East European Studies is recognized as a National Resource Center by the US Department of Education.
Program name: Russian and East European Studies, BA

description: Science, Technology, and Society (STSC) is a liberal arts major that focuses on one of the most important forces in modern life. The major prepares students to understand and participate in a world that is profoundly shaped by science and technology. It provides a strong foundation for citizenship, for careers in law, business, and public policy, as well as for graduate study in the humanities and social sciences. STSC courses analyze the historical, social, political, economic, and cultural dimensions of science, technology, and medicine. Some courses focus on the development of particular sciences or technologies, while others examine specific ethical or policy issues, such as those related to the internet, to health care, or to the environment. All students in the major learn how different disciplines in the humanities and social sciences study science and technology.

Concentration name: Cities, Communities, and Regions; Global, Transnational, and Comparative Sociology; Law and Society; Quantitative Methods; Sociology of Culture
description: Sociology is the study of the social lives of people, groups, and societies. It addresses the most challenging issues of our time, from the social causes and consequences of racism, poverty, crime, and environmental degradation to the social dynamics of business, technology, social media, and social movements. Sociology examines how social structures, institutions, and cultures are created and how they affect human action and social change. Sociology provides a unique understanding of how societies function and what can be done to address social problems.

The undergraduate major in South Asia Studies provides an excellent framework for understanding the history, cultures, and societies of this vast, diverse, and important part of the world. South Asia—which encompasses Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, the Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan, and Sri Lanka—is home to roughly one-quarter of the world’s population, two of the world’s major religions (Hinduism and Buddhism), one of the world’s largest Muslim populations, and a fascinating array of languages and cultural traditions. The major is broadly interdisciplinary, offering students the opportunity to explore this region from a wide variety of perspectives, including anthropology, archaeology, art history, cinema and media studies, history, history of art, literary and cultural studies, music, political science, religious studies, and sociology. As a part of the major, students are expected to gain proficiency in a South Asian language. The South Asia Studies major prepares students for graduate study as well as a range of professional careers, including education, government, international business, journalism, law, medicine, and non-profit/non-governmental organization (NGO) work.

Concentration name: Performance Concentration, Theatre and Performance Studies Concentration
description: The Theatre Arts major offers a unique opportunity for students to combine a rigorous, writing-intensive academic course of study with a diverse and challenging artistic practice. The major combines the study of dramatic literature, theatre history, performance theory and criticism, and performance practice within a liberal arts context. Courses embrace a broad spectrum of cross-cultural and interdisciplinary methods, and the faculty brings a wide range of expertise and artistic experience to the program. The major also provides opportunities for students to pursue intensive, pre-professional training in performance, design, and playwriting. Majors participate in an annual season of performances and events through the Theatre Arts Program and Penn Players Student Theatre, and are encouraged to take advantage of the numerous professional theatres located in Philadelphia. Courses in theatre provide credit towards the B.A. degree and are designed to develop students' critical and creative abilities and to expand their understanding of the relationship between theatre and society. Students graduating with a Theatre Arts major have successfully pursued advanced degrees at leading academic and professional training programs, as well as careers in the performing arts, film and television, arts management, casting, dramaturgy, law, education, business, and medicine. The Theatre Arts Program also offers a Minor in Theatre Arts and a Minor in Performance and is a partner in the Music Theatre Minor. Information on all three minors is available on the Theatre Arts website and elsewhere in the Catalog. The Theatre Arts Program is part of a collaborative relationship between the University of Pennsylvania and the Pig Iron Theatre Company, a partnership that supports professional training in devised performance. The Theatre Arts Program also engages in collaborative artistic and academic programming with a number of arts and culture organizations across campus.

Concentration name: Cities and Society; Urban Development and Commerce
description: The Urban Studies Program at the University of Pennsylvania offers a liberal arts-based, interdisciplinary approach to the study of urban life. The program draws on the social sciences and humanities, as well as the professional schools, to provide students with a broad-based understanding of cities and urban systems. A major in Urban Studies consists of twelve courses. Of these, six are the Urban Studies "core curriculum." The remaining six courses are an area of concentration that the student creates in conjunction with the Urban Studies academic advisor. The Urban Studies major has two concentrations: Cities and Society; and Urban Development and Commerce.

Visual Studies is an interdisciplinary undergraduate major in the College of Arts and Sciences that focuses on vision and visuality in the arts, humanities, and social, and natural sciences. The major consists of a variety of courses that are designed to develop visual literacy and critical seeing.

The Africana Studies minor offers an interdisciplinary approach to the study of the history, culture and social-political realities of Africans and people of African descent throughout the world. The curriculum seeks to provide students with a deep and broad understanding of the links between the social, economic, political and cultural dimensions of the Africana experience, including the creative expression of these experiences in literature, music, art and dance. The curriculum, therefore, highlights both the historical and contemporary experiences of Africans and their descendants in Africa, the U.S., the Caribbean and Latin America.

Concentration name: Law and Social Policy, Education Policy, Environmental Policy, Health Policy, Urban Policy and Community Development, Race and Ethnic Policy
description: The American Public Policy (APPC) minor focuses on the American political process and the analysis of U.S. public policy. It is designed to provide students with the analytic tools necessary for an understanding of the politics and economics of public policy and with in-depth exposure to at least one substantive policy area. Students will develop an understanding of how issues get on the political agenda, how political institutions and processes shape policy choices, and how the consequences of policy are evaluated. They will also gain an understanding of the economic justification for government intervention in the economy, and the potential for government failure. The minor requires a single course in statistics, one introductory course in either microeconomics or American politics, three courses from a list of core courses in public policy analysis and processes, and two courses in a substantive policy area such as education policy, health care policy, environmental policy, or urban policy.

The minor in American Sign Language and Deaf Studies, housed in the Department of Linguistics, consists of six course units. The minor gives students a comprehensive introduction to the language and culture of the Deaf community in the United States. Four courses are in the acquisition of American Sign Language (ASL), and two are in Deaf studies. These two courses are taught in English and have no pre-requisites.
Program name: American Sign Language and Deaf Studies Minor

description: Ancient history is an interdisciplinary field that draws on literary and material evidence to study the ancient Mediterranean world, from the second millennium BCE to (in some areas) the eighth century CE. It embraces a wide variety of cultures and regions, from Mesopotamia and the Near East through Egypt, Greece, and Rome, to the western provinces of the Roman empire. At Penn, ancient history is an interdepartmental major and minor jointly sponsored by the Departments of Classical Studies and History and administered through the Graduate Group in Ancient History.

The undergraduate minor in Archaeological Science provides students with a strong background in the scientific analysis of archaeological materials. Students will be exposed to the major methods used in archaeological science and will learn to interpret scientific data derived from archaeological finds in a theoretically-informed manner. Coursework introduces students to the major analytical tools available for scientific analysis of ancient artifacts and ecofacts, while required laboratory or field experience provides direct exposure to the practice of archaeological science. In consultation with the minor advisor, students may specialize in one of three major areas: archaeobotany (the analysis of ancient plant remains), zooarchaeology (the study of ancient animal remains), or the analysis of archaeological artifacts.

The Architectural History Minor is designed for students who want a broad-based introduction to the history of architecture, landscape architecture, and urbanism. The minor allows students to explore these histories from multiple disciplinary perspectives and to learn how to research and write about the built environment. It provides an especially strong basis for students interested in further graduate study in architectural history and theory, art history, historic preservation, and landscape studies.

The undergraduate minor in Architecture provides a broad introductory survey of the field of architecture in the context of a liberal arts education. It fosters an understanding of architecture as a cultural practice, a technological craft, and a profession. The program is designed for students who wish to gain a critical understanding of architecture and urbanism. The architecture minor also serves as an introduction for those students who plan to continue their education in architecture on a graduate level.

The Asian American Studies (ASAM) undergraduate minor offers an interdisciplinary approach to understanding the histories, communities, and contemporary experiences of Asians in the Americas. The program highlights the creative and intellectual productions of Asian Americans, as well as their social and political struggles. Students are encouraged to develop a comparative and critical perspective on Asian American experiences by taking courses in other ethnic studies programs, as well as by taking courses that place Asian Americans in a global and diasporic context. Through a broad range of courses in ethnic studies, the humanities and the social sciences, the minor in Asian American studies provides a strong foundation for students interested in a variety of fields and careers, including law, medicine and public health, social work, education, journalism, public policy, and arts and culture.

The undergraduate minor in Bioethics, offered through the Department of Medical Ethics and Health Policy at the Perelman School of Medicine, provides an opportunity for students to systematically study the ethical, legal, and social implications of advances in biomedicine and the life sciences. The minor requires six courses in bioethics. Course offerings range from the introductory "What is Bioethics?" to more advanced seminars on topics including clinical ethics, research ethics, neuroethics, law and ethics, and global health ethics. Students have the opportunity to count courses from departments and schools across the University. The Bioethics Minor is open to all undergraduate students at the University of Pennsylvania.

The undergraduate minor in biophysics is aimed at students with interests at the interface of physical and life sciences. The curriculum consists of a combination of core and elective courses in biology, chemistry, mathematics and physics, chosen to provide the breadth and depth required for this interdisciplinary field. The program is designed both for students who have a strong interest in biophysics but major in another subject, and for students who decide to major in biophysics late in their careers. It gives formal recognition to students who have made a serious commitment to biophysics.

The Chemistry Minor will provide students a strong background in the core aspects of chemistry, which could include organic, inorganic, physical, biological and materials chemistry. Chemistry is the central science and it provides the fundamental basis to understand biological processes, materials science, earth science and many other fields. This minor could serve as an excellent complement for majors in biology, physics, engineering, earth science, nursing or other majors in which a strong chemistry background will be beneficial for a future career.

The undergraduate minor in Cinema and Media Studies offers a structured, interdisciplinary curriculum, which is organized to provide a solid grounding in the history, theory, and aesthetics of film and media. The minor is offered to all undergraduate students in the College of Arts and Sciences, Wharton, Engineering, and Nursing.

The minor in Classical Studies is designed for students who want to become broadly familiar with the discipline of Classical Studies but do not have the time to devote to a full major. A student may minor in Classical Studies by taking any six courses in the department (CLST, GREK or LATN).

Cognitive science is the study of the human mind and its processes. An interdisciplinary field, it draws on many fields including psychology, linguistics, computer science, philosophy, and neuroscience. Students learn about the mind from many different levels, ranging from high-level tasks like reasoning and decision-making, to the neural mechanisms that subserve them. Research experience is an important part of the major, and students are strongly encouraged to work in a lab, whether it is for independent study course credit or on a volunteer basis. For more information please see the Cognitive Science Program website.

Comparative Literature is the study of literature and culture across linguistic, national and disciplinary boundaries. The program teaches students to think critically and write cogently about a wide variety of texts, from ancient philosophy to contemporary film. Courses are cross-listed in a wide variety of departments in the humanities and social sciences. The program provides an excellent foundation for graduate study in literature, theory, and cultural studies, as well as for professional training in law, journalism, publishing, and other fields.

The minor in Computational Neuroscience (CN) is designed for students interested in the computational principles that govern how we think, perceive, and act. The minor integrates a diverse, interdisciplinary set of courses from contributing departments including Biology (BIOL), Bioengineering (BE), Computer and Information Science (CIS), Electrical and Systems Engineering (ESE), Linguistics (LING), Mathematics (MATH), Philosophy (PHIL), Physics (PHYS), and Psychology (PSYC). Students will learn to use mathematical and computational tools to understand brain function and to probe the relationship between the brain and behavior. This minor will be especially attractive to students who have an interest in quantitative and computational approaches to studying the mind and brain, regardless of their major.

The Consumer Psychology Minor, offered by the School of Arts and Sciences and the Wharton School, is an interdisciplinary program that focuses on the psychological aspects of marketing and consumer behavior. Students who graduate with this minor will have a strong foundation for pursuing graduate studies or a career in marketing. The minor requires a total of 6 course units.

The Creative Writing Minor offers undergraduate students the opportunity to specialize in the writing of fiction, poetry, nonfiction, screenwriting, playwriting, and journalism. Through a series of workshops and seminars, students develop and hone their literary talents and creative skills. To complete the minor, students must take six courses from the Creative Writing Program's offerings, including at least three writing workshops. A maximum of one course may be taken in a related discipline, with the prior approval of the Creative Writing Program Director.

The Data Science & Analytics Minor is designed for students who want to develop a strong understanding of the principles and methods of data science and learn how to apply them to their own major fields of study. The minor will provide students with the foundational skills to collect, analyze, and interpret data, and to communicate their findings effectively. The minor is a joint program between the College of Arts and Sciences and the Wharton School, and is open to students from both schools.

The Digital Humanities Minor provides students with an introduction to the key questions, methods, and skills involved in the emerging field of digital humanities. It allows students to bring the analytical and conceptual tools of their home disciplines to bear on digital materials, and also to bring digital tools to bear on the objects of traditional humanities and social-scientific inquiry. The minor is highly interdisciplinary, and is open to students in all undergraduate schools at Penn. It offers students opportunities both for critical reflection on the digital and hands-on engagement with new technologies.

The East Asian Area Studies (EAAS) undergraduate program provides students with a comprehensive, interdisciplinary education in the humanities and social sciences focused on East Asia. This program combines the study of East Asian languages (Chinese, Japanese, and Korean) with a wide array of disciplinary and interdisciplinary courses. Students may major or minor in EAAS.
The EAAS undergraduate program prepares students for graduate study and for professional careers in many fields, including business, law, government, international relations, and cultural and educational institutions.

The East Asian Languages and Civilizations Minor enables students to focus on a particular country or region of East Asia—China, Japan, or Korea—and its language and culture.

The minor consists of 6 course units chosen in consultation with the Undergraduate Chair. Four of these must be language courses in Chinese, Japanese, or Korean, at or above the 2000-level/second year. The remaining two courses must be non-language EALC courses focused on the same country/region as the language courses. The two non-language courses must be at the 2000-level or above. First-year seminars may be counted toward this requirement with the approval of the Undergraduate Chair. Language courses taken at the 1000-level may not be counted for the minor.
Program name: East Asian Languages and Civilizations Minor

description: The Minor in East Central European Studies (ECES) is designed to provide students with a multi-disciplinary approach to the study of the lands and peoples between Germany and Russia. It focuses on the countries which since 1989 have experienced the most successful transition from communism to democratic free-market societies. These include Poland, the Czech Republic, Slovakia, and Hungary, but also the Baltic states, other Balkan countries, and Ukraine. Courses are offered in the social sciences and humanities by an interdisciplinary group of faculty who meet regularly in a faculty seminar.

The minor in Economic Policy is intended for students with an interest in public policy who wish to supplement their major with an understanding of economic analysis and its applications. The curriculum emphasizes the connection between economic principles and policy applications. The core of the minor is built around four required courses. Microeconomic theory is a prerequisite. Students choose two additional courses from an approved list of electives. The minor is administered by the Department of Economics in the School of Arts and Sciences.

The undergraduate minor in Economics is designed to provide students with a rigorous, broad, and critical understanding of the methods and ideas of modern economics. The minor will require students to complete the core intermediate-level theory courses (ECON 101 and ECON 102) and one course in econometrics (ECON 103). Students will then be able to choose two additional economics courses from a broad range of electives that reflect the great variety of questions that modern economics addresses. Some of the many areas in which economics minors may take courses are law and economics, development economics, finance, industrial organization, international economics, labor economics, and public economics. The minor is flexible enough to fit a wide range of interests and goals.

The English minor consists of six courses in English, all of which must be taken at Penn. A grade of C or better is required for a course to be counted towards the minor. No more than one creative writing workshop may be counted towards the minor. AP credit does not count towards the minor. Up to two courses taken abroad with an approved study abroad program may be counted toward the minor, with the approval of the Undergraduate Chair.

The undergraduate minor in Environmental Humanities (EHM) provides a coherent, interdisciplinary course of study for students interested in the relationship between the environment and human culture. This flexible minor gives students opportunities to delve into key concepts, including nature, culture, environment, and ecology, and to ask fundamental questions about the human place in the world. Courses in the minor address such questions through the lens of history, literature, philosophy, religion, anthropology, and the arts, while building an understanding of how these fields engage with the natural, social, and health sciences. Students pursuing the minor complete six courses, including one designated introductory course, four approved electives, and one capstone seminar. The EHM minor is excellent preparation for careers in environmental law and public policy, journalism, arts, and education.

The Environmental Science Minor provides a structured introduction to the scientific principles that are the foundation of understanding environmental issues. The curriculum provides a strong scientific background that prepares students to understand and address contemporary environmental challenges that often span multiple disciplines. The minor requires a core set of courses that provide an overview of environmental science, an introduction to key principles in geology, ecology, and chemistry, and a statistics course. Students must then complete three environmental science elective courses. Students are encouraged to pursue a cohesive theme in their electives, such as conservation, ecology, environmental chemistry, geology, marine science, or toxicology.

Concentration name: Sustainability and Environmental Management, Environmental Science, Environmental Humanities
description:
The minor in Environmental Studies (ENVS) is designed for students who wish to gain a deeper understanding of the scientific, social, and humanistic dimensions of environmental issues. Courses in this program reflect the interdisciplinary nature of the field and provide a foundation in the study of natural and human systems and the interactions between them.

The ENVS minor is administered by the Department of Earth and Environmental Science. Students are encouraged to develop a specific course of study in consultation with the Environmental Studies Undergraduate Advisor.

To best prepare for a major or minor in Environmental Studies, students should plan to take the introductory course, ENVS 1000 Introduction to Environmental Studies, early in their career. Students interested in the ENVS minor should see the Environmental Studies Undergraduate Advisor as soon as possible.

The minor in European Studies is designed to encourage students to think broadly about Europe in a comparative, interdisciplinary way. It will allow students with an interest in Europe to extend their knowledge beyond a single discipline by taking courses in multiple departments and programs. Administered by the Department of Germanic Languages and Literatures, the minor draws from departments and programs across the School of Arts and Sciences. With the guidance of the undergraduate chair, students will design their own curriculum of 6 course units to explore an area or topic of interest.

The undergraduate minor in Fine Arts is designed for students who are interested in the practice of visual arts. The minor is made up of a structured set of studio art and art history courses, which encourage each student to focus on one of the following areas: drawing, painting, sculpture, printmaking, photography, video and animation. The Weitzman School of Design Department of Fine Arts & Design administers this minor and provides an advisor for the students.

The French and Francophone Studies minor consists of six courses chosen in consultation with the Undergraduate Chair. Students may design a minor that focuses on literature, cinema, or cultural studies, or one that has a broader interdisciplinary focus. All courses must be taught in French. At least four of the six courses must be taken at Penn.

The Gender, Sexuality, and Women's Studies Program offers an interdisciplinary undergraduate minor that provides a critical, cross-cultural, and historical perspective on gender, sexuality, and women's issues. The Program provides students with the critical tools to analyze the construction and consequences of gender and sexuality categories in all areas of life, including the law, science, politics, the family, the workplace, art, and literature. Courses are offered by affiliated faculty from a wide variety of schools and departments including American Civilization, Anthropology, Art History, Cinema Studies, Communications, Comparative Literature, Criminology, East Asian Languages and Civilizations, Economics, English, Folklore, French, Germanic Languages and Literatures, Health and Societies, History, History and Sociology of Science, Legal Studies and Business Ethics, Music, Near Eastern Languages and Civilizations, Nursing, Philosophy, Political Science, Psychology, Religious Studies, Romance Languages, Slavic Languages and Literatures, Social Policy and Practice, and Sociology. Students may take courses from any of these departments to complete their major. For course descriptions, please see the GSWS website. Please consult the GSWS Program with any questions regarding courses.
Program name: Gender, Sexuality and Women's Studies Minor

description: The Geology minor requires 6 course units, as follows: EESC 2300, EESC 2400, or EESC 2500. Four additional courses, numbered EESC 2000 or higher. One course at any level.

The German minor consists of six courses. A student may receive credit for only one course in the GRMN 2000-2099 range. No more than two courses may be non-language courses. At least 3 CU must be taken at Penn. Students work with the undergraduate chair to design a course of study that best fits their interests. In addition to a wide range of courses offered by the department at the 2000- and 3000-levels, students may wish to take related courses in other departments such as History, History of Art, Jewish Studies, Music, Philosophy, and Political Science. Upon approval of the undergraduate chair, these courses may count towards the minor. Students should select an advisor from the undergraduate faculty. The department will also accept up to two transfer credits from study abroad programs per semester, with a limit of four CUs.

The Global Medieval Studies minor at Penn is an interdisciplinary program that draws on the expertise of faculty in a wide variety of departments and programs across the School of Arts and Sciences, as well as the professional schools and local institutions. The minor gives students the opportunity to learn about the major cultural and historical developments that took place across the globe during the thousand-year period from roughly 500 to 1500 CE. Students can focus on a particular region (Europe, the Middle East, East Asia), or on a particular theme or approach (manuscript studies, urbanism, literary history, etc.), but all students will gain a broad perspective on the medieval world and an understanding of the diversity of its cultures as well as the extent of its global interconnectedness.

The Hispanic Studies Minor consists of 6 course units. All courses must be taught in Spanish. A maximum of one course in translation can be approved by the Undergraduate Chair. Students may count a maximum of two courses taken abroad toward the minor. For courses to be accepted, they must be pre-approved by the Undergraduate Chair.

The study of history gives students a broad perspective on the human experience and develops the intellectual skills of critical thinking and cogent writing. Students of history learn to locate and evaluate primary sources, to assess and compare conflicting interpretations, to understand the complexity of causation, and to write analytical essays. An undergraduate education in history provides an excellent preparation for many careers, including law, journalism, business, public service, and education.

The Art History minor consists of six courses. In consultation with the undergraduate chair, students will devise a program that reflects their particular interests and provides a broad introduction to the history of art. At least four of the six courses must be taken at Penn.

The International Development minor provides students with the opportunity to take a diverse course of study centered around a common interest in understanding poverty, wealth, and inequality in the developing world. The minor is explicitly interdisciplinary and is organized thematically in order to allow students to construct a course of study that both reflects their own interests and exposes them to different methodological and theoretical approaches. Students will also fulfill the minor's fieldwork experience requirement, providing them with the opportunity to directly engage with the complex issues surrounding economic and social development within developing countries.

The International Relations Minor is intended for students who wish to supplement their major with a multidisciplinary approach to the study of international affairs. A total of 6 course units are required for the minor. Students must have a minimum GPA of 3.0 to be approved for the minor. At least 4 of the 6 course units must be taken at Penn.

The Italian Studies minor is designed for students who want to develop a strong command of the Italian language and to cultivate an in-depth knowledge of Italian literature and culture. It is an ideal course of study for students who have a general interest in Italian culture and for those who wish to complement their major with a strong background in Italian. The minor is a particularly valuable asset to students majoring in art history, classics, comparative literature, history, international relations, linguistics, music and political science.

The Jewish Studies Minor enables students to sample the offerings of the Jewish Studies Program and to design a course of study that reflects their own interests, whether they be in Jewish history, religion, literature, or culture. Students who complete the minor will have a basic understanding of the breadth of Jewish civilization and will also have studied one or more areas of Jewish Studies in-depth.

The Journalistic Writing minor, administered through the Center for Programs in Contemporary Writing (CPCW), is designed for students interested in developing the skills of a journalist: to report and write with accuracy and clarity, to find and incorporate sources, to work under deadline, and to tell a story in a way that is vivid and compelling. In courses offered through the CPCW, including the writing of fiction, poetry, nonfiction, and screenplays, as well as in courses focused specifically on journalistic writing, students will hone their abilities to convey information to a public audience through a variety of media. Students interested in the minor should seek the advice of the Director of Journalistic Writing, Dick Polman, who will help them select an appropriate sequence of courses.

The Landscape Studies Minor provides undergraduate students with a multi-disciplinary approach to the study of landscape. Students examine landscape as a textual, visual, and material practice. They engage with a range of methods and theories used in the analysis of landscape from the arts and sciences, including anthropology, archaeology, architecture, classics, fine arts, geology, history of art, historic preservation, and urban studies. The minor consists of six courses: a gateway seminar, LSTD 1640 Introduction to Landscape Studies; a methods course; and four electives.

The Latin American and Latinx Studies (LALS) Program offers an interdisciplinary minor designed to provide students with a multifaceted and nuanced understanding of Latin America, the Caribbean and people of Latin American descent in the United States and other parts of the world. Students in the minor focus on the histories, cultures, and contemporary socio-economic and political contexts of the region and its peoples. The program encourages a hemispheric and transnational framework, with a particular emphasis on the links that connect Latin America and the Caribbean to other regions of the world, especially Africa and North America. The LALS minor complements a wide variety of majors. It helps prepare students for careers in foreign service, law, government, business, journalism, social service, education, and research, among other professions.
Program name: Latin American and Latinx Studies Minor

description: Law is a crucial element of social, political and economic life, a feature of all human societies. The Law and Society minor is designed for students who wish to understand the nature of law, the problems to which law is addressed, and the role of law in society. The courses in the minor come from several departments in the arts and sciences, including anthropology, criminology, history, philosophy, political science, sociology and from the Wharton School. Students completing the minor will have an intellectually coherent, interdisciplinary introduction to the study of law and society.

The Legal Studies and History Minor is an interdisciplinary minor open to all undergraduate students in the College, Wharton, SEAS, and Nursing. This minor has been designed for students interested in the law from a liberal arts perspective.
