The minor allows students to explore the ways in which the law and legal institutions of the United States have developed and the ways in which they have reflected social, cultural, and political change over the course of American history. Students who are considering a legal career but who want to study law in an undergraduate, liberal arts context will find this minor particularly attractive. But the minor will be equally appropriate for any student interested in learning more about the role of the law in American history and society, whether or not that student is contemplating law school.

The Linguistics minor is designed for students who are interested in the nature of human language. Minors take a total of 6 course units, including a foundational course in linguistic analysis and a selection of more advanced courses covering the core areas of the field (sound structure, sentence structure, and meaning) as well as a variety of subfields and applications. The minor provides an excellent complement to a variety of majors in the humanities, social sciences, and natural sciences.

The Logic, Information, and Computation (LGIC) program is an interdisciplinary minor program that provides a formal and critical approach to computation and its applications in the digital age. This program brings together faculty from Computer and Information Science, Linguistics, Mathematics and Philosophy to teach in an integrated curriculum. It is a supplement, not a substitute, for a major in one of the participating disciplines. The curriculum is intended to prepare students for graduate work and for a variety of careers.

The undergraduate minor in Mathematics is designed to give students a strong background in the fundamentals of theoretical mathematics. Students interested in the minor should consult the undergraduate chair as early as possible.

The Medical Sociology minor provides an opportunity to examine the social context of health, illness, and medical care. The curriculum gives students a sociological perspective, which is becoming increasingly important for a broad range of professional fields, including medicine, public health, hospital administration, medical law, and health policy. Medical sociologists study the social causes and patterns of health and disease; the social behavior of health care personnel and their patients; the social functions of health organizations and institutions; and the social patterns of the utilization of health services.

The Modern Middle Eastern Studies (MMES) undergraduate minor is designed to provide students with a broad, multi-disciplinary understanding of the modern Middle East, a region understood as stretching from Morocco to Afghanistan and including the Arab world, Iran, Israel, and Turkey. The coursework for the minor exposes students to a variety of disciplines and methodologies, with an emphasis on the social sciences and humanities. While language study is not required for the minor, MMES minors are strongly encouraged to achieve proficiency in a Middle Eastern language, such as Arabic, Hebrew, Persian, or Turkish.

The Music Minor is designed for students with a serious interest in music who wish to combine it with another major field of study. Students minoring in music should consult with the Undergraduate Chair in Music to plan their course of study as early as possible. A minimum of 6 course units is required.

The undergraduate minor in Native American and Indigenous Studies (NAIS) introduces students to the core concepts, questions, and methods of the interdisciplinary field of Native American and Indigenous studies. Students in the NAIS minor will gain an understanding of the diversity of Indigenous cultures, histories, and languages in the Americas; the history and ongoing legacies of colonialism in the Americas; Indigenous epistemologies, spiritual traditions, and cultural practices; Indigenous intellectual traditions, including Indigenous scholarship and Indigenous traditional knowledges; and the politics and legal status of Indigenous peoples in the United States and internationally. Students can tailor the minor to meet their interests by choosing to focus on specific topics, time periods, Indigenous cultures, and/or geographic areas. The NAIS minor prepares students to apply their knowledge in fields such as education, law, public history, health, medicine, business, and public policy, and to pursue graduate studies in a number of fields.
Program name: Native American and Indigenous Studies Minor

description: The minor in Middle Eastern Languages and Cultures (MELC) provides students with the opportunity to learn about the histories and cultures of the Middle East while gaining proficiency in one of its languages (Arabic, Hebrew, Persian, or Turkish). The minor is particularly well suited for students with an interest in the history, politics, religions, and cultures of the region, including those planning a career in which knowledge of the Middle East would be an asset. Many MELC minors have successfully combined their expertise in the region with majors in political science, history, religious studies, international relations, and business.
Program name: Middle Eastern Languages and Cultures Minor

description: The Neuroscience Minor provides an opportunity for students to learn about the brain and nervous system from an interdisciplinary perspective. The minor exposes students to a variety of topics and levels of analysis in the field of neuroscience and is complementary to a wide range of majors.

Concentration name: Basic Nutrition Science Track, Nutrition in the Life Cycle Track
description: The Nutrition Science Minor, offered by the School of Nursing, provides students with a foundation in the science of nutrition and its application to health. The minor offers two tracks, the Basic Nutrition Science Track and the Nutrition in the Life Cycle Track, each of which provides an in-depth look at specific aspects of nutrition science. The minor will be of particular interest to students in the life sciences, as well as those planning careers in the health professions, but is open to all undergraduate students.

The Physics minor consists of 6 courses. Two course units are required from the introductory physics sequence. The PHYS 0150-PHYS 0151 sequence is recommended, especially for those students contemplating a major in the sciences or engineering. Four additional courses are chosen from PHYS 0200 and above, including at least two courses from PHYS 0300 and above. PHYS 0495 is not allowed for the minor.

The Psychoanalytic Studies Minor offers undergraduates the opportunity to pursue an interdisciplinary course of study that focuses on the theory, application, and history of psychoanalysis. From its origins in the clinical neurology of the nineteenth century, psychoanalysis has had a revolutionary and enduring impact across the humanities, arts, and social sciences. As a theory of the mind, a method of inquiry and interpretation, and a therapeutic practice, psychoanalysis has transformed modern and contemporary understandings of human subjectivity, meaning, and motivation. The minor introduces students to the foundational texts and concepts of psychoanalysis and then allows them to explore its influence across a wide range of disciplines, including history, literature, film, politics, and gender and sexuality studies. The minor also helps prepare students interested in pursuing clinical careers in psychology, social work, and medicine.

The Psychology Minor introduces students to the main areas of this discipline. A student minoring in psychology takes an introductory course (PSYC 0001), 2 courses from the foundational areas of the major (one from the Biological Science distribution and one from the Social Science distribution), and 3 additional courses of their choosing in Psychology. A minimum of 4 courses must be taken at Penn. A minimum of 4 courses must be taken in the Psychology Department. Students should speak to the Undergraduate Coordinator in Psychology to declare the minor.

The Religious Studies Minor offers students an opportunity to explore the vital role that religion plays in human societies. The minor is interdisciplinary. Our faculty have been trained in a variety of fields, including anthropology, history, sociology, textual studies, and philosophy, and our courses are cross-listed in a wide variety of departments. The minor offers a great deal of flexibility, enabling students to devise a program of study that is well-suited to their interests. The undergraduate chair is happy to assist students in this task.

The Russian and East European Studies (REES) major and minor introduce students to a strategically important and culturally rich region of the world: Russia, Ukraine, and other post-soviet states; Poland, the Czech and Slovak Republics, and other states of the former socialist bloc; and the diasporas of these countries.
Program name: Russian and East European Studies Minor

description: The undergraduate minor in Science, Technology and Society (STSC) is designed to give students a sophisticated understanding of how science, technology and medicine are shaping our modern world. Courses in the minor focus on the social, cultural, political, economic and ethical dimensions of science, technology and medicine, in the past and in the present. The minor provides a strong interdisciplinary foundation for students who plan careers that engage with science and technology, as well as in business, law, and medicine.

Sociology is the study of the social lives of people, groups, and societies. Its subject matter is our own behavior as social beings. Sociology offers a distinctive and enlightening way of seeing and understanding the social world in which we live and which shapes our lives. It is the study of social structure and social change, and the causes and consequences of human behavior.

The South Asia Studies minor provides an opportunity for students to gain a broad, multidisciplinary perspective on the history, culture, and political economy of South Asia. The curriculum includes courses on the arts, humanities, and social sciences.

The Statistics minor provides a broad-based foundation in statistical concepts, methods, and practice, as well as the opportunity to develop the specialized skills needed to analyze large, complex, and high-dimensional data. This minor is not open to students who are majors or minors in Mathematical Economics, Actuarial Mathematics, majors in Networked and Social Systems Engineering, or majors in Computer and Information Science.

The Penn Program on Opinion Research and Election Studies (PORES) offers a minor in Survey Research and Data Analytics. The minor is open to all Penn undergraduates and provides students with the opportunity to develop a deep, theoretically-grounded understanding of public opinion and data analysis, combined with practical training in the methods and techniques that are used in the real world of polling and survey research. The minor is meant for students with interests in survey methodology, data analytics, public opinion, and/or elections. Students will become critical consumers of survey research and data analytics, as well as have the ability to conduct their own original data-based research.
Program name: Survey Research and Data Analytics (PORES) Minor

Concentration name: Sustainability and Business, Sustainability and Policy, Environmental Science, Global Sustainability, Urban Sustainability
description: The Sustainability and Environmental Management minor prepares students to address the complex issues of how to develop a sustainable society in a world with a rapidly growing population and a finite resource base. Students learn to use scientific principles and an interdisciplinary approach to analyze environmental problems and develop effective solutions. The minor also gives students an opportunity to focus their coursework on a subject of interest by choosing from a list of five themes that contain both natural and social science courses. The five themes are Sustainability and Business; Sustainability and Policy; Environmental Science; Global Sustainability; and Urban Sustainability. The minor requires a total of 6 course units.

The Theatre Arts Minor provides a foundation for students interested in performance and theatre studies. Students who minor in Theatre Arts have opportunities to perform, write, direct, design, manage, and dramaturg productions under the guidance of a faculty of artists and scholars. The Theatre Arts Minor is open to all undergraduate students in the College of Arts and Sciences, the School of Engineering and Applied Science, the School of Nursing, and the Wharton School.

The Urban Education Minor (UEM) is a cross-school, interdisciplinary minor for Penn undergraduate students who are interested in the study of urban education. Housed in the Graduate School of Education, the UEM offers courses taught by faculty from across the University, including GSE, SAS, SP2, and Wharton. The minor introduces students to the field of urban education and to research, theory, and practice related to it. In addition to coursework, students in the minor engage in a semester-long field placement through an Academically Based Community Service (ABCS) course, working in West Philadelphia schools. The UEM has four requirements (for a total of 6 course units).

The Urban Real Estate and Development minor is intended for students who are interested in the study of real estate in the urban context. The minor will provide students with the opportunity to develop a fundamental understanding of real estate markets, real estate development, real estate law and public policy, real estate finance, and urban and metropolitan economic and demographic trends. Real estate is one of the world's most important asset classes, and the business of real estate impacts all aspects of urban life. The minor combines coursework from real estate, urban studies, urban design and planning, and related fields to enable students to study real estate from an interdisciplinary perspective. The curriculum examines the institutional, financial, and regulatory contexts that shape real estate markets and the process of real estate development in cities, how the market for urban real estate works, and how public policies can promote economic and social well-being.
Program name: Urban Real Estate and Development Minor

description: The Urban Studies minor provides undergraduates with an opportunity to study the city and the metropolitan region from an interdisciplinary perspective. The minor's courses, drawn from across the social sciences and humanities, focus on urban society and culture; urban history; and urban politics, policy and economics. Through its courses and field-based research, the minor seeks to develop in students the capacity to understand urban phenomena and to do so comparatively. The Minor is comprised of six courses. A student's program must be approved by the Urban Studies Associate Director.
